newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Political fur flies over Sarajevo utility problem.
newsitem.headline: Political fur flies over Sarajevo utility problem.

text.p: Sarajevans are wrestling with gas, water and electricity shortages for the fifth winter in a row, and watching as the international community and the Bosnian government blame one another for the problem.

War was the clear cause of shortages in past years as separatist Serbs besieging Bosnia's capital cut supplies and forced residents to root out tree stumps for firewood, queue for water and huddle in darkened flats for months on end.
But a year after the Dayton peace agreement was signed and after a billion dollars in reconstruction aid and other foreign expenditures, the city is still plagued by outages.

Bosnian Prime Minister Hasan Muratovic has been blaming the international community and its top civilian representative Carl Bildt, saying donor bureaucracy and related political conditions are causing the problem.
Normally imperturbable, Bildt has responded by laying the mess at Muratovic's doorstep in blunt, undiplomatic language.
Bildt's office says "significant shortcomings" in the way the Bosnian authorities are handling the post-war economic and social situation in the country are responsible.

"We do not accept that these authorities try to put the blame for their own shortcoming on us...There has been an unprecedented amount of economic assistance given to Bosnia this year," Bildt's spokesman Colum Murphy said on Thursday.
"It is our view that there is no real reason why there should be inadequate gas, heating, electricity, water, basic supplies reaching the ordinary people of Sarajevo."

World Bank sources say Sarajevo's gas shortage stems from the government not having paid its bill to Russia over the past year and is not the result of rival Bosnian Serb authorities cutting the supply as they did in the past.
On the issue of water shortages, Colum Murphy also put the responsibility on the Bosnian government.
"There really isn't any great reason why Sarajevo, built as it is on springs in the mountains, surrounded by mountain streams, should ever be short of water," he said.
International agencies say the Bosnian government bureaucracy often fails to act even in its own self-interest.
The U.N. refugee agency spent the last half-year trying to purchase duty-free fuel from the Bosnian government so its trucks could continue aid deliveries.
"In six months they have not replied to our request...and in the meantime we have run out of fuel," U.N. spokesman Kris Janowski explained on Thursday.
"Now we are arranging to get fuel from (NATO) for the most basic deliveries of humanitarian aid. This illustrates the absurdity of the situation."

Observers say heated exchanges between Muratovic and Bildt should be seen as the prelude to tough negotiations in London next week when the international community meets to fine-tune the Dayton peace process as it heads into its second year.
As the political fur flies, Sarajevans soldier on. "Sure it's cold in my flat but at least nobody's shooting at us," said Nino, a 27-year old baker.
"I don't know who's to blame for the problem this winter but I bet they have gas and electricity where they live."
